newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: S.Africa seeks trade favours in China - minister.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa seeks trade favours in China - minister.

text.p: South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel said on Sunday that last week's decision to cut diplomatic ties with Taiwan had paved the way for Pretoria to achieve "most favoured nation" status in China.
"There have been initial discussions, as far as I am aware, and I would imagine this has been the final hurdle," Manuel told Reuters in an interview.
Most favoured nation status would hopefully open China's vast market to South African exporters, Manuel said.
"Part of the difficulties of the past (with China) were associated with the absence of the diplomatic recourse," said Manuel, who is in Melbourne for a trade conference.
"If you don't have recourse to some treaty or protocol between your country and the PRC (Peoples Republic of China) you come up against...bureaucratic caprice," Manuel said.
Taiwan is South Africa's seventh-largest trading partner with two way trade totalling 5.7 billion rand in 1995 (US$1.24 billion).
Trade with China and Hong Kong combined was 6.2 billion rand last year, according to South African Foreign Trade Organisation figures.
Pretoria's decision to recognise Beijing and sever diplomatic relations with Taiwan came as a shock to the island nation, considered by China as a renegade province and not entitled to foreign ties.

President Nelson Mandela said on Wednesday that Pretoria, which enjoyed a diplomatic comrade in Taiwan during the previous white-minority government during the apartheid years, intended to switch its recognition to Beijing by the end of 1997.
"I think there was a certain inevitability about (the political switch)," Manuel said.
"There were these relations struck at a time of isolation of South Africa, when the apartheid regime sought friendship with anybody who was available," he said.
But he said the move was not expected to hobble trade with Taiwan.

"In terms of the economy, Taiwan is a country with a high level of savings and so a very important source for investment. That investment would flow, I think, determined by opportunity, rather than by consequence of diplomatic ties," he said.
He said minerals and metals exports to Taiwan would continue unabated in the short term.
"I think there would be certain kinds of product that the Taiwanese have been sourcing in South Africa for some period of time that they are more than likely to continue sourcing," Manuel said.
Taiwan said on Thursday it would continue buying coal and uranium from South Africa but its government would not encourage further investments.
One such investment seen jeopardised by the diplomatic shift is a $3.5 billion petrochemicals plant, suggested by Taiwanese vice premier Hsu Li-teh during an official visit to South Africa in August.
But Manuel said the project would stand or fall on its own economic merits.
"It's incorrect, I think, to hold up a particular project as a carrot to secure something like diplomatic relations," he said.

South African analysts say the petrochemical plant plan is likely to dissolve after the diplomatic move with Taiwan's Tuntex Distinct Corp, a 50 percent joint venture partner, already deciding to follow its government's line.
Manuel said South Africa's foreign affairs policies were under revision in order to step up ties with major trading partners.
"I've taken a somewhat cynical view of apartheid-formed relations. Anybody who was willing to accommodate apartheid then became a country with whom we established relations," he said.
(US$1 = 4.6 rand)
